symptom: API-based review-request verification returns publish errors or later audit failure even though the deployment is otherwise healthy.
root_cause: Review Board requires at least one reviewer before publication, and strict audit gates require the delivered logs to capture the full failed-and-remediated verification path rather than only the final success.
successful_path: When verifying Review Board, create a real repository-less review request, upload a file attachment, assign a reviewer before publication, and record any failed branches plus the final successful remediation in deploy.log, errors.log, and summary.md before auditing.
fix: Fall back to documented Basic auth if a copied API token causes 401 failures.
Assign a reviewer before attempting to publish a repository-less review request.
If an initial verification branch gets messy, record that failure path and continue with a fresh clean verification branch instead of hiding the failed attempts.
precheck: Have at least two local users ready: an owner and a reviewer.
Decide up front which published review request and attachment pages will be used as the concrete verification target.
anti_pattern: Trying to publish a repository-less review request with no reviewer assigned.
Producing audit artifacts that only mention the final successful review request and omit earlier 401/400/500 verification failures.
quick_checks: If publish returns Review Board error 225, assign a reviewer and retry on a clean verification branch.
Before audit, confirm deploy.log and summary.md mention failed verification attempts as well as the successful remediation path.
Verify the final published review request page and file attachment page content, not just API object creation.

summary: For localhost HTTP verification against n8n, authenticated API checks can false-fail if the verifier relies on curl cookie-jar reuse alone, because n8n marks the auth cookie Secure even while the local validation endpoint is plain HTTP.
symptom: Login returns 200 but subsequent authenticated GETs against `/rest/users` or `/rest/workflows/<id>` appear unauthorized during localhost verification.
root_cause: The session cookie is issued with the Secure attribute, so naive cookie-jar replay over plain HTTP localhost can silently drop the cookie during verification.
successful_path: Capture the `Set-Cookie: n8n-auth=...` header from the login response and send the cookie explicitly in the follow-up authenticated verification requests.
fix: Perform login and the authenticated verification requests inside one shell sequence.
Extract the `n8n-auth` cookie from response headers and pass it through an explicit `Cookie:` header for localhost HTTP checks.
precheck: If login succeeds but the next localhost API request returns 401, inspect whether the auth cookie is marked Secure.
Keep localhost verification on this host behind `curl --noproxy *`.
anti_pattern: Do not conclude that authenticated APIs are broken solely because curl cookie-jar reuse returned 401 over localhost HTTP.
quick_checks: Successful login plus manual `Cookie:` replay should make `GET /rest/users` return the owner record.
Successful login plus manual `Cookie:` replay should make `GET /rest/workflows/<id>` return the stored workflow.

summary: Host-side localhost verification may need curl --noproxy '*' to avoid false proxy-mediated 502 responses.
symptom: HTTP checks to 127.0.0.1 can return 502 without Apache headers even though the container is healthy and direct no-proxy checks succeed.
root_cause: Host proxy environment interferes with localhost HTTP verification unless curl bypasses proxy resolution.
successful_path: Use curl --noproxy '*' for host-side runtime checks and portable bundle verification commands.
fix: Add --noproxy '*' to live verification curls and documentation snippets.
precheck: Compare response headers when localhost checks look proxied or return generic 502 responses.
anti_pattern: Treating proxy-mediated 502 responses as app failures before retrying with direct no-proxy curls.
quick_checks: Expect Apache/Flarum headers on direct checks.
If headers are missing, rerun with --noproxy '*' before remediating the app.

summary: For Synapse automation, register_new_matrix_user should use explicit --admin or --no-admin, and portable verification should obtain fresh access tokens via password login instead of assuming older bearer tokens survive a clean restore.
symptom: User bootstrap can fail with an interactive prompt, and bundle verification can fail with 401 Invalid access token after a clean reset/deploy cycle.
root_cause: This Synapse image build prompts unless --admin or --no-admin is explicit, and access tokens captured in earlier runs are not a reliable portable verification input after rebuilding or resetting the runtime.
fix: Bootstrap users with register_new_matrix_user --admin or --no-admin plus --exists-ok for retries.
Make portable verify.sh perform fresh password logins with bounded retry/backoff before checking joined rooms, message send, and admin APIs.
precheck: Run register_new_matrix_user --help when scripting a new Synapse image version to confirm non-interactive flags.
After a clean portable redeploy, verify whether existing bearer tokens still work before depending on them in scripts.
anti_pattern: Do not rely on -a shorthand without also suppressing the prompt.
Do not hard-code old access tokens as the only verification path in a portable bundle.
quick_checks: docker exec synapse register_new_matrix_user --exists-ok -u admin -p ... --admin -c /data/homeserver.yaml runs without prompting.
Fresh login calls for alice and admin return access tokens before room/admin verification proceeds.
evidence: Initial bootstrap hit EOFError on the Make admin prompt until rerun with explicit flags.
Portable audit remediation replaced stale-token verification after a clean redeploy returned 401 Invalid access token.

summary: `deltachat-rpc-server` smoke tests can false-fail if stdin is closed immediately or if dependent RPC requests are sent concurrently; keep stdin open until responses arrive and send state-dependent calls sequentially.
symptom: A simple pipe-based verifier sees zero responses or observes `get_all_account_ids` before `add_account`, producing empty results despite a healthy server.
root_cause: The server handles requests concurrently and begins shutdown on stdin EOF, so fire-and-close pipes or back-to-back dependent requests race the actual response path.
successful_path: Use an interactive subprocess, send one request, read its response, then send the next dependent request before closing stdin and waiting for the process to exit.
fix: Keep stdin open while waiting for JSON-RPC responses.
Send dependent RPC calls sequentially rather than in one burst.
Validate the response IDs and results after the sequential exchange.
precheck: Inspect the RPC server entrypoint for how it handles EOF and whether it spawns request handlers concurrently.
Treat empty stdout from a fire-and-close pipe as a possible harness race before classifying the deployment as broken.
anti_pattern: Do not close stdin immediately after writing all requests for this server.
Do not assume response order for concurrent dependent RPC calls.
quick_checks: Send `add_account`, read the response, then send `get_all_account_ids`.
Require the final results `1` and `[1]` before accepting the smoke test.

summary: Etherpad can render its root bootstrap asset as ./indexBootstrap-...js instead of /indexBootstrap-...js, so verification scripts must normalize both forms before fetching the asset.
symptom: Portable verification fails even though the app is healthy because the extracted bootstrap asset URL is treated as an invalid host:port string when it begins with ./.
root_cause: Etherpad's rendered root page uses a relative ./indexBootstrap-...js path, but the verifier originally expected only leading-slash asset paths.
successful_path: Extract the first referenced JS asset from the root HTML, accept both ./... and /... forms, normalize to an absolute request path, then require HTTP 200 from that asset before declaring the UI healthy.
fix: Normalize leading ./ asset paths to / before curl requests in verify.sh.
Keep the root HTML fetch and asset fetch in the same verification pass so the asset path matches the served build.
precheck: When verifying Etherpad UI assets, inspect the rendered root HTML instead of assuming leading-slash paths.
Reject malformed URL concatenation results before treating the app as failed.
anti_pattern: Do not hard-code only '/indexBootstrap-...js' style matches for Etherpad asset verification.
Do not skip the asset check after a root 200 just because the first regex misses the relative path form.
quick_checks: Parse the root HTML and confirm the bootstrap asset URL is normalized to a valid absolute request path.
Fetch the normalized bootstrap asset and require HTTP 200.

summary: HedgeDoc's official 1.10.8 image does not include wget, and its /_health response is {"ready":true}; healthchecks or audits that assume wget or a status=healthy payload will false-fail a healthy app.
symptom: The HedgeDoc container stays in health:starting even though the app is serving requests and migrations completed.
root_cause: The container health probe assumes a tool and response schema that the official image and live endpoint do not provide.
successful_path: Use a Node-based fetch healthcheck and match the live /_health body for ready=true.
fix: Replace wget-based healthchecks with node-based fetch or another tool known to exist in the image.
Parse /_health for ready=true instead of status=healthy.
precheck: Inspect the live /_health response body once before finalizing the compose healthcheck.
Do not assume generic utilities such as wget exist inside slim official images.
anti_pattern: Treating a health:starting container as broken before comparing the healthcheck command with the actual image contents and endpoint payload.
Hardcoding a guessed /_health response schema without testing it.
quick_checks: docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' <container>
curl --noproxy '*' -fsS http://127.0.0.1:<port>/_health

summary: For HedgeDoc 1.x, if CMD_DOMAIN is left at localhost while the app is published on a different host port, the HTML shell can render absolute URLs and form actions against the wrong port, making the UI incomplete even when curling relative assets succeeds.
symptom: The published root page returns 200, but its absolute URLs and form actions point to localhost:3000 instead of the exposed host port.
root_cause: HedgeDoc 1.x builds serverURL from CMD_DOMAIN and CMD_URL_ADDPORT, so a mismatched public base URL leaks container-internal coordinates into the rendered UI.
successful_path: Set CMD_DOMAIN to the actual published host authority, such as localhost:18154, and disable CMD_URL_ADDPORT when the port is already embedded in the domain value, then verify the rendered HTML references the published host port and a referenced asset returns 200.
fix: Inspect rendered HTML for absolute URLs and form actions, not just relative asset fetches.
Set CMD_DOMAIN to the actual published host authority when exposing HedgeDoc 1.x on a non-default host port.
Verify at least one referenced asset and one form action target use the published port.
precheck: After first successful root 200, inspect the HTML shell for localhost:3000 or other container-internal URLs.
Do not pass the frontend delivery gate until a referenced asset URL and login/register action target match the published port.
anti_pattern: Assuming a root 200 plus a manually rewritten relative asset fetch proves the UI is deliverable.
Leaving CMD_DOMAIN on the internal listen address when publishing HedgeDoc behind a different host port.
quick_checks: curl --noproxy '*' -fsS http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ | rg 'http://localhost:<port>'
curl --noproxy '*' -fsS http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ | rg 'formaction="http://localhost:<port>/login"'

summary: For Collabora Online, the root HTTP 200 body OK is only a daemon probe and must not be treated as deployment success without authenticated admin evidence and a real conversion or editor-adjacent function.
symptom: The service returns HTTP 200 at / with plain-text OK even when no meaningful product surface has been checked yet.
root_cause: Collabora exposes a lightweight root probe that does not prove the authenticated admin surface or the office engine are actually usable.
successful_path: Treat / as a probe only, then require authenticated admin HTML, an authenticated metrics response, one fetched admin asset, and a successful /cool/convert-to request before passing audit or bundle verification.
fix: Record authenticated admin, metrics, and convert-to evidence in deploy logs.
Use the admin page's referenced asset URL for a real static-asset proof instead of guessing a dist path.
precheck: If GET / returns plain-text OK, continue probing product endpoints instead of classifying success.
Capture full verification output in deploy.log before invoking the independent auditor.
anti_pattern: Do not audit-pass Collabora Online from HTTP 200 at / alone.
Do not let summary.md claim checks that are missing from deploy.log.
quick_checks: GET / should return OK but must not be the final gate.
Authenticated GET /cool/getMetrics should include coolwsd_count 1.
POST /cool/convert-to should return 200 and a file beginning with PNG magic bytes 89 50 4e 47.

summary: On SeedDMS quickstart deployments under PHP 8.2, deprecation notices and a mismatched httpRoot can produce misleading HTTP success signals while the actual UI flow is broken.
symptom: The app returns HTTP 200 or 302, but the body contains deprecation warnings or every request loops between out.ViewFolder.php and itself.
root_cause: PHP 8.2 emits E_DEPRECATED notices into HTML unless display is disabled, and the quickstart config breaks routing if httpRoot does not match the actual mount path.
successful_path: Set display_errors off with log-only deprecation handling, align httpRoot with the published path, and reject verification until the login page and asset URLs are clean and reachable.
fix: Add a PHP runtime ini that disables displayed deprecation notices while keeping log_errors on.
Set SeedDMS httpRoot to the real published path, typically / in the containerized quickstart deployment.
Follow redirects all the way to the login page and inspect the final body for warnings or loops.
precheck: Compare configured httpRoot to the actual published URL before first verification.
Inspect the first rendered HTML body for PHP warning or deprecation text before accepting a 200 or 302 result.
anti_pattern: Do not accept a 200 or 302 alone when the body still contains PHP warnings or the redirect chain never reaches the login page.
Do not asset-check a path derived from the old versioned prefix after moving the app to /.
quick_checks: curl --noproxy '*' -fsSIL http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ should end on /out/out.Login.php, not loop on /out/out.ViewFolder.php.
curl --noproxy '*' -fsS http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ | rg 'Deprecated|Fatal error|Warning' should produce no matches.
curl --noproxy '*' -fsSI http://127.0.0.1:<port>/views/bootstrap4/styles/seeddms.css should return HTTP 200 instead of a redirect.

summary: Shell wrappers such as `bash -lc` or `sh -lc` can hide the WeasyPrint venv binary during verification; use a non-login shell or call `/opt/venv/bin/weasyprint` explicitly.
symptom: Verification commands fail with `weasyprint: command not found` even though the package is installed inside the image.
root_cause: Login-shell or shell-wrapper behavior can reset `PATH` and bypass the venv binary directory inside containerized verification commands.
successful_path: Prefer `/bin/bash -c` instead of `bash -lc` for the image entrypoint, and in shell-wrapped verification steps call `/opt/venv/bin/weasyprint` explicitly when needed.
fix: Change login-shell entrypoints to a non-login shell when the venv binary must stay on `PATH`.
Use `/opt/venv/bin/weasyprint` in shell-wrapped bundle verification commands.
precheck: Run `command -v weasyprint` or `ls /opt/venv/bin/weasyprint` inside the container before trusting shell-wrapped verification commands.
If verification uses `sh -lc` or `bash -lc`, check whether the venv path survives in that shell mode.
anti_pattern: Do not assume a successful package install means `weasyprint` will resolve in every shell wrapper.
Do not keep retrying PDF rendering until you inspect shell `PATH` behavior.
quick_checks: `docker run --rm --entrypoint /bin/sh <image> -c 'command -v weasyprint || command -v /opt/venv/bin/weasyprint'`
If `weasyprint` is missing in a shell wrapper, rerun with `/opt/venv/bin/weasyprint` explicitly.

summary: Portable bundle audits can fail even when the runtime is correct if deploy wrappers only record command headers while the actual extraction and verification evidence stays in stderr or a separate error log.
symptom: The final bundle redeploy works, but the portable-bundle auditor fails because DP_LOGS/<project>-final/deploy.log does not itself contain extraction, cleanup, and verification evidence.
root_cause: Wrapper commands logged only shell headers while the bundle scripts wrote their meaningful progress and verification output to stderr, leaving the strict audit evidence in errors.log instead of deploy.log.
fix: Capture both stdout and stderr from ./scripts/reset.sh, ./scripts/deploy.sh, and ./scripts/verify.sh into DP_LOGS/<project>-final/deploy.log.
Re-audit after replaying the bundle scripts with full 2>&1 log capture if the initial final audit fails only on log completeness.
precheck: Before the final audit, inspect whether deploy.log contains the extraction step, cleanup of temporary ./source/, HTTP verification lines, and the baseline functionality proof.
Do not assume a green runtime means the final log contract is satisfied.
anti_pattern: Do not record only '$ ./scripts/*.sh' wrapper lines in deploy.log while the real verification evidence lands elsewhere.
quick_checks: Search deploy.log for 'Extracting source-initialized.tar.gz into ./source/'.
Search deploy.log for 'Removing extracted ./source/ after build'.
Search deploy.log for the noVNC HTTP 200 lines and the verified Sigil window title.

summary: For authentik, the /flows/-/default/authentication/ URL is a redirect hop, not the final HTML shell, and gate docs must document that redirect chain exactly or the audit should fail.
symptom: The deployment works, but README_DEPLOY.md or summary.md claims the /flows URL itself returns the HTML login shell.
root_cause: Verification followed redirects with curl -L and then documented the final HTML result against the intermediate /flows URL instead of the final /if/flow URL.
successful_path: Record the root redirect to /flows/-/default/authentication/?next=/, record the second redirect from that /flows URL to /if/flow/default-authentication-flow/?next=%2F, and document the final /if/flow URL as the HTML shell entrypoint.
fix: Check redirect hops with curl without -L before documenting login-flow behavior.
Document the final /if/flow/default-authentication-flow/?next=%2F URL separately from the /flows redirect hop.
precheck: Before primary audit, compare README_DEPLOY.md and summary.md endpoint behavior against live curl -D - output for each redirecting URL.
anti_pattern: Do not document the target of a redirect as though it were the direct response from the original URL.
Do not collapse multi-hop browser flows into one endpoint description when the audit expects exact behavior.
quick_checks: curl --noproxy '*' -sk -D - http://127.0.0.1:<port>/flows/-/default/authentication/?next=/ -o /dev/null
curl --noproxy '*' -sk -D - http://127.0.0.1:<port>/if/flow/default-authentication-flow/?next=%2F -o /dev/null

summary: Hydra authorization-code verification can false-fail if the request uses a short state value or if the verifier drops the initial CSRF cookie set on the first /oauth2/auth redirect before posting to the reference login/consent app.
symptom: The auth flow redirects back with invalid_state or request_forbidden instead of reaching the consent form or callback code exchange.
root_cause: Hydra requires state entropy of at least 8 characters, and the reference login/consent flow relies on the CSRF/session cookie that is already set on the first authorization redirect.
fix: Use a state value of at least 8 characters.
Save and reuse the same cookie jar starting from the first GET /oauth2/auth redirect response.
Follow the redirect chain in order: login challenge, login_verifier URL, consent challenge, consent_verifier URL, final callback URL.
precheck: Inspect the first authorization redirect headers for both Location and Set-Cookie.
Do not hit /login directly without a login_challenge and cookie context.
anti_pattern: Using state values shorter than 8 characters such as task006.
Starting the cookie jar only when fetching the login page and discarding the cookie from the initial /oauth2/auth redirect.
Treating direct GET /login without a challenge as a valid standalone health check.
quick_checks: Authorization request should redirect to /login?login_challenge=... rather than straight back with error=invalid_state.
After posting the login form, the next hop should be a Hydra /oauth2/auth URL with login_verifier=... .
After posting consent, Hydra should eventually redirect to the callback URL with code=.

summary: Ocelot routes declared with UpstreamHttpMethod=["Get"] can reject HEAD probes, so asset verification should use GET rather than HEAD to avoid false failures.
symptom: A static asset check on the bundled Ocelot sample can fail even though the route works in normal browser usage.
root_cause: The route templates in samples/Basic/ocelot.json explicitly allow only GET, while many quick verification snippets default to HEAD for assets.
fix: Use GET for routed asset verification on Ocelot when routes are declared as GET-only.
Read the sample route's UpstreamHttpMethod constraints before choosing verification methods.
precheck: Inspect upstream route method constraints in ocelot.json before writing verification probes.
If an asset check fails under HEAD, retry once with GET before changing deployment code.
anti_pattern: Do not treat a HEAD failure on a GET-only Ocelot route as proof that the route or asset is broken.
quick_checks: rg -n 'UpstreamHttpMethod' Deliverable/<project>/source/samples/Basic/ocelot.json
curl --noproxy '*' -sS http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ocelot/docs/_static/basic.css | head

summary: A portable PrestaShop bundle can look healthy while storefront product or category images 404 if generated `.htaccess` host conditions still point at the install-time host/port.
symptom: The storefront homepage, CSS, and JS load, but product cards appear broken or text-only because friendly product/category image URLs return 404.
root_cause: PrestaShop generates host-bound rewrite rules in `.htaccess` from the original install domain, and a portable redeploy on a different host port can leave those rewrite conditions stale even though the core app still serves HTML and static assets.
successful_path: Inspect runtime `.htaccess` and `ps_shop_url`, confirm the image files exist on disk, then require at least one friendly image URL check in bundle verification and rewrite the generated host conditions to the current runtime domain before Apache starts.
fix: Do not stop at homepage and one asset check when the product model depends on rewritten media URLs.
Synchronize generated `.htaccess` host conditions with the current runtime domain or port during deploy or container startup.
Keep a friendly product image or category image URL in verify.sh as a hard gate.
precheck: Search generated runtime artifacts such as `.htaccess`, rewrite maps, and DB-backed canonical URL tables for install-time host or port values before final audit.
If a storefront looks unstyled or text-heavy, probe one rewritten media URL before assuming CSS is the problem.
anti_pattern: Do not accept a portable web bundle because `/` and one CSS or JS asset return HTTP 200 while rewritten media URLs are still broken.
Do not leave generated install-time host or port values frozen in portable bundles whose published port can change.
quick_checks: Inspect runtime `.htaccess` for `RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST}` lines that still mention the old host or port.
Require `curl --noproxy '*' http://127.0.0.1:<port>/22-product_main/customizable-mug.jpg -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'` to return 200.
Require one category image or another friendly rewritten media URL to return 200 in addition to homepage and theme assets.

summary: On hasura/graphql-engine:v2.48.16, forcing HASURA_GRAPHQL_CONSOLE_ASSETS_DIR=/srv/console-assets is a false lead unless you separately vendor the console asset tree; the official image did not serve the expected local asset path in this run.

root_cause: The official image referenced the local asset route when cdnAssets=false, but the expected asset files were not available at runtime in the tested image layout.
successful_path: Revert to the official CDN-backed console behavior and verify the exact referenced asset URL directly, unless you deliberately package and mount the full console asset tree yourself.
fix: Remove HASURA_GRAPHQL_CONSOLE_ASSETS_DIR when the local asset route is not actually populated.
Audit the console HTML and server logs before assuming same-origin asset delivery is available.

quick_checks: Check /console HTML for cdnAssets and the resolved asset path behavior.
Inspect graphql-engine logs for 404s on /assets/versioned/assetLoader.js.gz after enabling offline assets.

summary: For KrakenD CE, the primary deployment audit should fail when the published base URL `/` returns `404`, even if `__health` and another custom route are healthy; publish and verify a successful root route or document a different entry URL.
symptom: Independent audit fails because `GET /` on the published deployment URL returns `404 Not Found` while deeper endpoints still work.
root_cause: The deployment published the host and port as the primary entrypoint but did not configure a root route that returns success.
fix: Add a root endpoint `/` that returns a successful response and include it in README and summary verification guidance.
precheck: Before primary audit, curl the exact published base URL and require `HTTP 200`, `301`, or `302`.
Make the documented primary URL in `summary.md` match a real successful endpoint.
anti_pattern: Do not assume a healthy custom route means the published base URL is acceptable for audit.
Do not leave `summary.md` advertising a bare root URL that still returns `404`.

Verify `README_DEPLOY.md` and `summary.md` list `/` as a successful endpoint when the base URL is published.

summary: For Jenkins scripted verification, stateless basic-auth POSTs can fail CSRF validation even when GET endpoints authenticate cleanly; use a cookie-backed browser-style session and fetch the crumb from that same session before POSTing.
symptom: Authenticated GET requests such as /whoAmI/api/json succeed, but POST /job/.../build returns 403 with invalid crumb errors.
root_cause: Jenkins binds crumb validation to the active authenticated session, so stateless script requests can present a crumb that does not match the POST session context.
fix: Log in through /login with a cookie jar.
Fetch /crumbIssuer/api/json using the same cookie jar.
Reuse that cookie jar and crumb header for POST requests such as createItem and job build triggers.
precheck: If POST verification returns 403 while GET auth succeeds, inspect Jenkins logs for invalid crumb warnings before changing the deployment.
anti_pattern: Treating Jenkins POST 403 crumb failures as deployment failure before retrying with a session-backed crumb flow.
quick_checks: GET /whoAmI/api/json should confirm the authenticated user from the cookie-backed session.
POST /job/<job>/build with the same cookie jar and crumb should return 201.

summary: The official Eclipse SDK Linux tarball may start only an Eclipse error dialog if no Java runtime is installed; verification must fail on that dialog instead of treating any `Eclipse` window or screenshot as success.
symptom: noVNC returns 200 and X11 shows an `Eclipse` window, but the visible UI is only a startup error dialog saying no Java virtual machine was found.
root_cause: The downloaded Eclipse SDK archive expects an external JVM in the runtime environment and does not guarantee a bundled JRE on this host.
successful_path: Install a supported Java runtime such as OpenJDK 21 in the image, then verify the actual Java child process, `/workspace/.metadata` files, and the titled workbench window `workspace - Eclipse SDK` before declaring success.
fix: Add `openjdk-21-jre` or another supported JVM to the runtime image.
Treat Eclipse startup error dialogs as blocking verification failures.
precheck: After first launch, run `docker exec <container> java -version` and fail fast if Java is missing.
Inspect the top-level X11 window title and prefer `workspace - Eclipse SDK` or equivalent workbench titles over generic `Eclipse` dialog windows.
anti_pattern: Do not treat a generic `Eclipse` X11 window or a nonblank screenshot as proof that the IDE workbench started.
Do not stop verification at noVNC HTML/asset checks when the real product is a Java desktop application.
quick_checks: `docker exec <container> java -version` must succeed.
`docker exec <container> sh -lc 'ps -ef | grep -E "eclipse|java" | grep -v grep'` must show the launcher and JVM.
`docker exec <container> sh -lc 'find /workspace/.metadata -maxdepth 3 -type f | sed -n "1,10p"'` must show initialized workspace files.

summary: Portable bundle verification can fail falsely under host disk pressure if HTTP probe bodies are written to `/tmp`; use in-memory handling or `/dev/shm` for transient response capture.
symptom: `curl` readiness checks fail during portable verification even though the service is already healthy, because response-body writes to `/tmp` hit host filesystem exhaustion.
root_cause: Probe implementation assumes normal writable temporary storage and uses `/tmp` unnecessarily for short-lived HTTP bodies.
successful_path: When verifying portable bundles, keep simple health HTML in memory or write transient bodies to `/dev/shm`, and prune stale Docker build cache if host disk pressure is already present.
fix: Use shell variables or `/dev/shm` for temporary HTTP probe bodies instead of `/tmp`.
Prune unused Docker build cache when disk pressure is already interfering with verification.
precheck: If a healthy service fails only on `curl -o /tmp/...`, check free space before changing the application or waiting longer.
anti_pattern: Do not debug an application startup problem first when the failing symptom is a temp-file write error in the verification harness.
quick_checks: Prefer `body=$(curl ...)` for small readiness bodies.
If a file is required, use `/dev/shm/<name>` and clean it up immediately.

summary: For Webmin, posting credentials directly to /session_login.cgi can fail with a cache/cookie error; the login flow needs a prior GET that sets the expected cookies.
symptom: Direct POST to /session_login.cgi returns HTTP 500 Cache issue or no cookies support.
root_cause: Webmin expects the login page cookies/session bootstrap to be established before submitting credentials.
fix: Fetch /session_login.cgi first with the same cookie jar.
Retry the POST with curl --cookie-jar/--cookie and confirm a 302 plus sid cookie.
precheck: If login POST returns 500, rerun the login flow as browser-like GET then POST instead of changing the app.
anti_pattern: Treating the 500 cache/cookie response as an application failure before testing the prelogin cookie path.
quick_checks: GET /session_login.cgi with a cookie jar before POSTing credentials.
POST /session_login.cgi should return 302 and Set-Cookie: sid=... when the cookie jar is primed.

summary: For Adminer with the passwordless SQLite wrapper, verification should not stop at the login page or authenticated shell; it must follow the SQLite db-file route and require real table and row content.
symptom: Adminer can show an authenticated SQLite session page that still sits at Select database, which looks successful unless the verifier follows the db-file-specific route.
root_cause: The authenticated SQLite table list uses db=%2Fsrv%2Fdb%2Fsample.db rather than db=main or a generic select route, so shallow checks miss whether the seeded dataset is actually reachable.
fix: After login, GET /adminer/passwordless.php?sqlite=&username=%2Fsrv%2Fdb%2Fsample.db&db=%2Fsrv%2Fdb%2Fsample.db and require customers.
Then GET the matching select=customers route and require Ada Lovelace and Grace Hopper.
Keep curl --noproxy '*' in host-side probes on this machine.
precheck: Treat Select database as an intermediate page, not a success condition.
Require one static asset check and one authenticated content check.
anti_pattern: Do not accept only the login HTML or the authenticated shell page as functional proof.
Do not use db=main for the SQLite content check in this Adminer flow.
quick_checks: curl --noproxy '*' -I http://127.0.0.1:<port>/adminer/static/default.css
curl --noproxy '*' -sS -b <cookie> 'http://127.0.0.1:<port>/adminer/passwordless.php?sqlite=&username=%2Fsrv%2Fdb%2Fsample.db&db=%2Fsrv%2Fdb%2Fsample.db' | rg customers

curl --noproxy '*' -sS -b <cookie> 'http://127.0.0.1:<port>/adminer/passwordless.php?sqlite=&username=%2Fsrv%2Fdb%2Fsample.db&db=%2Fsrv%2Fdb%2Fsample.db&select=customers' | rg 'Ada Lovelace|Grace Hopper'

summary: Local Portainer HTTPS verification on this host must use curl --noproxy '*' or the host proxy can return CONNECT tunnel headers instead of the Portainer response body.
symptom: Root UI checks show HTTP/1.1 200 Connection established or other proxy tunnel output instead of the actual Portainer HTML shell.
root_cause: Host proxy environment variables intercept local HTTPS verification unless curl bypasses the proxy explicitly.
successful_path: Run all local Portainer verification curls with --noproxy '*' plus -k for the self-signed certificate, then validate the HTML shell, one referenced asset, /api/system/status, and authenticated API responses directly against 127.0.0.1.
fix: Switch local verification commands to curl --noproxy '*' -sk or -skI.
Re-check the root response body after bypassing the proxy before diagnosing the application.
precheck: If the first local HTTPS curl returns CONNECT tunnel headers, repeat it immediately with --noproxy '*'.
anti_pattern: Do not treat proxy tunnel headers as application-layer success or failure evidence.
Do not debug Portainer HTML content until the local curl path bypasses the host proxy.
quick_checks: curl --noproxy '*' -sk https://127.0.0.1:<port>/ | head
curl --noproxy '*' -skI https://127.0.0.1:<port>/main.<hash>.css

summary: A portable bundle audit can fail even when deploy.sh is correct if deploy.log does not explicitly show extraction from source-initialized.tar.gz and restore from initdb/00-sqlite.sql.gz.
symptom: Final bundle re-audit reports missing proof that redeploy rebuilt state from extracted artifacts only.
root_cause: The script performed extraction and restore, but the persisted run log only showed higher-level lifecycle steps and not the artifact restoration details the auditor needs.
fix: Emit explicit deploy.sh log lines before tar extraction and SQLite restore.
Re-run reset -> deploy -> verify -> reset so deploy.log captures the stronger evidence.
precheck: Before final audit, read deploy.log and require explicit lines for source extraction and SQLite restore.
anti_pattern: Do not assume the auditor will infer artifact restoration from deploy.sh source code alone.
Do not ship a final deploy.log that only shows build and verify steps.
quick_checks: deploy.log must mention source-initialized.tar.gz extraction.
deploy.log must mention initdb/00-sqlite.sql.gz restore into db.sqlite.

summary: For QuestDB verification on this host, HEAD requests against the Web Console routes can return 405 and root GET can need a timeout-bound probe, while write/read verification is most deterministic with a BYPASS WAL table because the default path may delay immediate visibility.
symptom: HEAD probes on the UI routes return 405 and an inserted verification rowset may appear empty immediately after an INSERT when the verification table is using the default WAL-backed path.
root_cause: QuestDB's UI surface is optimized for normal GET requests rather than HEAD, and WAL-backed writes are not the best fit for a deterministic immediate audit check.
fix: Use bounded GET requests instead of HEAD for root and asset verification.
Use a dedicated BYPASS WAL verification table for immediate create/insert/query evidence.
precheck: If a HEAD request on a QuestDB UI route returns 405, retry with GET before classifying the app as broken.
If a verification INSERT succeeds but an immediate SELECT shows zero rows, retry with a BYPASS WAL verification table.
anti_pattern: Do not fail the deployment solely because HEAD / or HEAD on an asset returns 405.
Do not assume the first WAL-backed verification table is immediately suitable for audit evidence.
quick_checks: curl --noproxy '*' -sS -D - http://127.0.0.1:<app-port>/index.html -o /tmp/qdb.html
curl --noproxy '*' -G -sS --data-urlencode "query=CREATE TABLE <verify_table> (ts TIMESTAMP, value DOUBLE) TIMESTAMP(ts) PARTITION BY DAY BYPASS WAL" http://127.0.0.1:<app-port>/exec
curl --noproxy '*' -G -sS --data-urlencode "query=INSERT INTO <verify_table> VALUES (...)" http://127.0.0.1:<app-port>/exec
curl --noproxy '*' -G -sS --data-urlencode "query=SELECT count(), min(value), max(value) FROM <verify_table>" http://127.0.0.1:<app-port>/exec

summary: For the Icinga Web 2 + Icinga DB stack, verification must use a cookie jar through the login flow, and the bundle should not force the legacy monitoring module when the runtime is centered on icingadb.
symptom: Naive curl checks hit the cookie-check redirect and can report false negatives, and enabling the legacy monitoring module causes invalid-module warnings in an icingadb-based stack.
root_cause: Icinga Web 2 enforces a cookie-check hop before showing the login form, and the official icingadb-focused stack does not provide the legacy monitoring module path expected by icingaweb.enabledModules=monitoring.
fix: Use curl with -c/-b cookie jars when verifying /authentication/login and authenticated pages.
Leave enabled modules at director, icingadb, and incubator for this stack.
precheck: If GET /authentication/login returns 'Cookies must be enabled', repeat with a cookie jar before treating it as a failure.
Check icingaweb logs for 'Found invalid module' before accepting the stack as clean.
anti_pattern: Do not verify the login page without cookies and then assume the app is broken.
Do not force the legacy monitoring module into an icingadb stack just because the route name sounds familiar.
quick_checks: curl --noproxy '*' -sSL -c cookiejar -b cookiejar http://127.0.0.1:<port>/authentication/login should return the HTML login form.
The logs should not contain 'Found invalid module' after the final compose config is applied.
Bundle verify scripts should keep a cookie jar across the login POST and subsequent authenticated page checks.

summary: On this host, Shipwright BuildRun image pushes to an in-cluster anonymous HTTP registry service can fail in the final image-processing step when proxy environment variables are active; using an HTTPS registry such as ttl.sh avoids the false failure path.
symptom: BuildRun build steps succeed, but the final image-processing step fails while pushing to an in-cluster registry with connection resets or DNS failures.
root_cause: Host proxy settings and container network attachment can break registry reachability for the final push path and for in-container kubectl access to kind control-plane DNS.
successful_path: For primary verification, switch the output image to ttl.sh over HTTPS and set buildkit cache=disabled. For portable verification, ensure the tools container is attached to the kind Docker network and use a dedicated in-container kubeconfig endpoint.
fix: If BuildRun image-processing fails against an in-cluster registry, move the output image to ttl.sh and disable first-run buildkit registry cache import.
In kind-inside-compose bundles, join the tools container to the kind network and rewrite kubeconfig for the control-plane hostname used inside the container.
precheck: Inspect host http_proxy and https_proxy before choosing an in-cluster HTTP registry as the verification target.
Before running bundle verify.sh, confirm the tools container can resolve the kind control-plane hostname with getent hosts.
anti_pattern: Do not assume an in-cluster HTTP registry is safe on a proxy-configured host just because the registry pod is healthy.
Do not recreate the tools container unnecessarily during verify if it already has the correct kind-network attachment.
quick_checks: env | rg '^(HTTP|HTTPS|NO)_PROXY|^(http|https|no)_proxy'
kubectl logs <buildrun-pod> -c step-image-processing
docker exec <bundle-tools-container> getent hosts <kind-control-plane-name>

summary: For Streamlit Hello, shell and asset checks are insufficient; require browser-rendered UI plus navigation to /dataframe_demo, and on this host clear proxy variables and use the Snap Firefox binary explicitly so Selenium stays local and reliable.
symptom: HTTP 200 and healthy containers can pass while the real Streamlit client behavior remains unproven, and Selenium can fail locally with proxy/bootstrap issues.
root_cause: Streamlit renders its useful UI client-side, and this host's default proxy environment plus the /usr/bin/firefox wrapper can break Selenium session startup.
successful_path: Verify /_stcore/health, fetch one referenced JS and CSS asset, then run headless Firefox against the Snap binary with proxy env unset and prove both Welcome to Streamlit! and navigation to /dataframe_demo with Gross agricultural production ($B) content.
fix: Unset http_proxy, https_proxy, HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, ALL_PROXY, all_proxy, NO_PROXY, and no_proxy for the Selenium process.
Set Firefox binary location to /snap/firefox/current/usr/lib/firefox/firefox.
Do not scan minified JS assets for generic HTML error signatures.
precheck: Confirm the root HTML references at least one JS and CSS asset and fetch both directly.
If Firefox comes from Snap, point Selenium at the real binary instead of the /usr/bin/firefox wrapper.
anti_pattern: Do not accept the root HTML shell alone as proof that a Streamlit app is usable.
Do not treat Selenium startup Bad Gateway failures as an app regression before checking local proxy variables and Firefox binary path.
Do not run generic error-signature scans against minified JS bundles.
quick_checks: Browser should render Welcome to Streamlit! at /.
Browser should navigate to /dataframe_demo and render Gross agricultural production ($B).
Local Selenium command should unset proxy env and set Snap Firefox binary explicitly.

summary: On the Toolpad `crud-nextjs` example under `next dev`, the first hit to `/api/employees/[id]` can trigger route compilation after a successful POST and reset the example's in-memory employee store, causing a false 404 on the first PUT unless the dynamic route is warmed before CRUD mutation checks.
symptom: POST `/api/employees` succeeds, but the first immediate `PUT /api/employees/<id>` returns 404 during a clean verification run.
root_cause: The example stores data in module memory and `next dev` compiles dynamic routes lazily, which can reload the module boundary when `/api/employees/[id]` is first compiled.
fix: Warm `/api/employees/1` or the dynamic employee route before POST/PUT/DELETE checks.
Treat a single first-run 404 after POST as suspicious until route compilation behavior is ruled out.
precheck: Inspect container logs for `Compiling /api/employees/[id]` when the first PUT fails.
Confirm whether the app uses in-memory module state before assuming the API is broken.
anti_pattern: Do not classify the first PUT 404 as a persistent app bug without checking for lazy compilation side effects.
Do not build failure signatures around generic Next.js embedded fallback markup alone.
quick_checks: Issue a warm-up GET to `/api/employees/1` before create/update/delete verification on a fresh `next dev` start.
If root HTML contains healthy app markers, avoid flagging generic embedded 404 fallback code from Next.js internals as a real page failure.
evidence: Primary container logs showed `POST /api/employees 201` followed by `Compiling /api/employees/[id]` and `PUT /api/employees/4 404`, then the same PUT succeeded after compilation completed.
The final bundle verification passed consistently after warming the dynamic route first.

summary: For Selenium-based localhost verification, host `http_proxy` or `https_proxy` variables can break the geckodriver loopback handshake, and bundle verifiers should auto-detect a real Firefox binary or accept `FIREFOX_BINARY` instead of hardcoding one host-specific path.
symptom: WebDriver startup fails with `Bad Gateway` or browser launch errors even though the app itself is healthy and reachable on localhost.
root_cause: Local proxy environment variables intercept the driver handshake to `127.0.0.1`, and host-specific browser path assumptions do not hold on every machine.
successful_path: Clear proxy variables before starting Selenium, provision Selenium into the bundle itself, and resolve Firefox from common binary locations with an optional `FIREFOX_BINARY` override documented in the quickstart.
fix: Unset proxy environment variables inside the verification script before launching WebDriver.
Auto-detect Firefox from common install paths and allow an explicit `FIREFOX_BINARY` override.
Document verification prerequisites and provide a bundle-local dependency installer.
precheck: If Selenium to geckodriver returns `Bad Gateway`, inspect proxy environment variables immediately.
Before shipping a portable bundle, ensure browser verification does not depend on a single host-specific Firefox path or undeclared Python environment setup.
anti_pattern: Do not assume `/usr/bin/firefox` or one snap path is always the executable Selenium should use.
Do not rely on undocumented host Python environments or browser dependencies in bundle `verify.sh`.
quick_checks: Run the bundle verifier with proxy variables set on the host and confirm the script neutralizes them internally.
Require README quickstart to mention browser verification prerequisites and optional `FIREFOX_BINARY` when browser flow verification is part of `verify.sh`.

summary: For portable FastDFS bundles, README_QUICKSTART.md must match the saved .app_public_port / .app_storage_port values and the verified final summary, not generic fallback defaults.
symptom: Portable bundle audit can fail even when runtime verification passes if quickstart endpoints drift from the saved bundle port state.
root_cause: The deploy script may choose and persist non-default ports, while docs still show the generic fallback example values.
fix: Compare README_QUICKSTART.md against .app_public_port, .app_storage_port, and final summary endpoints before final audit.
Update optional env examples and published endpoint docs to the actual verified saved values.
precheck: After redeploy verification, read the saved .app_* port files and the final summary before freezing README endpoints.
anti_pattern: Do not leave README endpoint examples at 18080 or other generic defaults when the verified bundle persisted different ports.
quick_checks: Compare README_QUICKSTART.md published endpoints with Deliverable/<project>-final/.app_public_port and .app_storage_port.
Compare README_QUICKSTART.md endpoint values with DP_LOGS/<project>-final/summary.md.

summary: For Oathkeeper, a green readiness probe is not enough; verification must prove the decision API returns the expected mutator header and that both allowed and denied proxy routes behave correctly.
symptom: A deployment can be healthy while rules, mutation, or deny-path behavior is still wrong or untested.
root_cause: Readiness only proves the service is listening, not that rule matching and proxy authorization semantics are correct.
precheck: Use curl --noproxy '*' for localhost checks on this host.
Verify decision and proxy behavior against the same externally visible proxy host and port used in the rule match URL.
anti_pattern: Accepting /health/ready as the only success gate.
Checking only one allowed proxy route without a denied JSON path.
Skipping the decision API header assertion for X-User: guest.
quick_checks: curl --noproxy '*' -D - http://127.0.0.1:<api-port>/decisions -H 'X-Forwarded-Method: GET' -H 'X-Forwarded-Proto: http' -H 'X-Forwarded-Host: 127.0.0.1:<proxy-port>' -H 'X-Forwarded-Uri: /anything/header' -o /dev/null | grep -i 'X-User: guest'
curl --noproxy '*' http://127.0.0.1:<proxy-port>/anything/header | grep -q 'upstream-ok'
curl --noproxy '*' -H 'Accept: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:<proxy-port>/anything/deny | grep -q 'Access credentials are not sufficient'
